10.1002_adfm.202415035: Anisotropic volume changes in primary particles of layered Ni‐rich transition metal oxides generate mechanical stresses during electrochemical cycling. This results in structural degradation and side reactions that deteriorate battery performance. To address this issue, a cross‐linked epoxy natural rubber (CENR) is employed as the protective elastomeric interphase. The viscoelastic properties of CENR facilitated a strong adhesion to the surface of Ni‐rich cathodes, thereby helping alleviate mechanical stresses during cycling. This approach maintained the structural integrity of the Ni‐rich cathodes and suppressed detrimental interfacial reactions. Consequently, the fortified Ni‐rich cathode retained 95.9% of its capacity after 300 cycles at 0.5 C and 82.8% after 500 cycles at 1 C. This study highlights the essential role of elastomeric materials in stabilizing Ni‐rich cathodes and offers insights that can enable the development of additional protective elastomeric layers for battery electrode materials.
10.1002_adfm.202525912: Hydroxyl groups on advanced material catalysts typically facilitate catalytic reactions, especially in formaldehyde (HCHO) oxidation, where active hydroxyl species are crucial to the rate‐determining step, with water vapor often promoting the reactivity. However, this study observed a completely opposite effect. A hydroxy‐rich palladium/silicon dioxide catalyst (Pd/SiO 2 (H)) displayed reduced performance in HCHO oxidation under water vapor conditions, attributed to pronounced surface hydrophilicity and hydroxyl‐mediated electron depletion in Pd species, which impaired water dissociation capability. In contrast, the hydroxyl‐deficient SiO 2 support (named as SiO 2 (L)) exhibited strong interaction with loaded Pd particles, resulting in electron enrichment of the Pd species. This electronic modification enhanced the water dissociation capability, generating reactive hydroxyl species, which facilitated HCHO oxidation reactions. Combined in situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (in situ DRIFTS) analysis and density functional theory (DFT) calculations revealed the preferential adsorption of HCHO at Pd‐Si(OH) interfacial sites, following a direct formate oxidation pathway ([HCHO] → [HCOO] → [CO 2 ] + [H 2 O]). In addition to the above pathway, on hydroxyl‐deficient Pd/SiO 2 (L) catalyst, HCHO primarily adsorbs on metallic Pd particles, proceeding via a formyl (HCO) decomposition pathway ([HCHO] → [HCO] → [CO] + [H]). This study provides robust theoretical guidance for the directed design of advanced materials.
10.1002_adfm.202570037: Lithium Metal Anodes In article number 2413958, Johannes Kasnatscheew and co-workers present bi-directional crosstalk phenomena within Li-based batteries, i.e., (1) from cathode to anode via transition metals and (2) from anode to cathode via solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) components. The latter, the “inverse crosstalk”, is severe for Li anodes and can thicken cathode electrolyte interphases (CEI), but is shown to have low impact on resistance and battery performance.
10.1002_advs.76607: Silicon suboxide (SiO x ) has attracted significant attention as a promising anode material for next‐generation lithium‐ion batteries due to its high capacity and improved structural stability. However, precise control over stoichiometry and pore structure remains challenging under conventional thermal annealing. Herein, we introduce an empirical‐aided active learning (EAAL) approach to optimize high‐throughput laser‐induced photothermal annealing of high‐performance SiO x anodes. By synergistically combining probabilistic machine learning with empirical domain knowledge, the EAAL framework efficiently explores complex processing parameter spaces using a limited number of experiments. Remarkably, the EAAL‐optimized anode achieves electrochemical performance comparable to that of an empirically optimized counterpart while significantly reducing the number of laser irradiation passes from five to two, thereby improving practical production throughput in cumulative laser‐processing. Furthermore, the optimal conditions are identified using only 26 experimental data points, significantly improving process efficiency. This study demonstrates a data‐efficient strategy for process optimization by synergistically integrating machine learning with empirical domain knowledge and provides a scalable pathway for the advanced manufacturing of high‐performance energy storage materials.
10.1002_smll.76533: Achieving high ionic conductivity of wet‐synthesized sulfide solid electrolytes remains a critical challenge for enabling scalable all‐solid‐state batteries (ASSBs). In Cl‐rich Li‐argyrodites, Li + transport is strongly governed by the Cl occupancy at the 4d Wyckoff site, yet conventional wet syntheses fail to control this local structure due to the spontaneous formation of unfavorable intermediate phases. Here, we uncover that the formation of the PS 3 Cl 2− moiety during intermediate heat‐treatment stages suppresses 4d‐site Cl incorporation, thereby limiting ionic conductivity. By introducing controlled amounts of S 8 as a reaction‐kinetic modulator, we show that S–S‐containing precursor environments kinetically hinder PS 3 Cl 2− formation during heat treatment. Multimodal structural analyses (solid‐state NMR, XRD Rietveld refinement, DSC) confirm that increasing S 8 systematically increases 4d‐site Cl occupancy while suppressing the undesired intermediate. This kinetic steering enables the Li 5.5 PS 4.5 Cl 1.5 (LPSCl 1.5 ) electrolyte to reach a high ionic conductivity of 6.06 ± 0.29 mS cm −1 at 25°C without additional specialized processing such as rapid thermal annealing or spark plasma sintering. ASSB half‐cells incorporating this electrolyte exhibit excellent rate capability and 77.8% capacity retention over 500 cycles at 2 C. This work establishes a mechanistic framework for intermediate‐phase engineering in wet synthesis and presents a high‐performance wet‐synthesis route with potential for scale‐up.
10.1021_acs.analchem.6c05043: Electrochemiluminescence (ECL) bioassays are essential for rapid intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) diagnosis, while conventional approaches require bulky instrumentation and complex readout electronics that hinder point-of-care (POC) use. To address this limitation, we developed a battery-driven catalysis-initiated ECL imaging platform for multiplexed detection of ICH-associated microRNAs. The device integrated a gold film-modified copper microneedle array (Au film/Cu MNA), polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) dual-chamber microcells, and button-battery excitation. Heterogeneous catalysis at the Au film/Cu MNA generated reactive oxygen species (ROS) that amplified ECL and sustained luminescence propagation across 168 μm. A competitive hybridization assay using ferrocene-modified linker DNA (Fc-LDNA) on microneedle tips enabled simultaneous miRNA-126 and miRNA-21 detection with detection limits of 4.6 and 0.8 pM, respectively. A hybrid convolutional neural network (CNN) model decoded spatial emission patterns, extending the linear ranges to 1.28 ∼ 32 fM and 0.59 ∼ 32 fM, beyond those achieved by pixel averaging. Preliminary clinical validation (n = 35 ICH, n = 25 healthy controls) revealed an inverse miRNA expression correlation and dual-target diagnostic accuracy (AUC = 0.993), exceeding single-biomarker performance (miRNA-126: AUC = 0.945; miRNA-21: AUC = 0.964). This strategy advances ECL bioanalysis toward portable, multiplexed biomarker quantification in neurological and inflammatory diseases.

10.1073_pnas.2613985123: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) persist in aquatic environments due to their ultrastable C–F bonds and poor susceptibility to conventional treatment. Here, we report an H 2 -based catalytic-film membrane that enables PFAS destruction in ambient conditions by generating highly reactive surface (H ads * ) and subsurface hydrogen (H sub * ), the latter stored as β-phase palladium hydride (β-PdHx). Solid-state analyses evidenced β-PdHx formation and related lattice expansion with elevated H 2 chemical potential, revealing a structural mechanism that links hydrogen storage to catalytic defluorination. Mechanistically, the two hydrogen species play complementary roles: H ads * -rich Pd 0 surface enabled PFAS capture through parallel adsorption to maximize interfacial contact with active H, whereas sustained H sub * supplied the energetic driving force for stepwise hydrodefluorination consistent with sequential C–F scission. As a result, across six PFAS of regulatory concern—PFOA, PFOS, PFNA, PFHxS, PFBS, and GenX—the catalytic membrane converted all contaminants toward fully defluorinated products. Long-chain PFAS were removed and defluorinated more rapidly than short-chain analogs, while GenX showed greater recalcitrance due to its ether linkage, weaker adsorption, and higher average C–F bond dissociation energy; nonetheless, GenX still exhibited removal and defluorination, with the production of 2-propoxypropanoic acid. The system also enabled continuous coremoval of all six PFAS in ambient conditions, with up to 96% removal and 83% defluorination over 58 d. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for how active hydrogen is generated, stored, and deployed in catalytic membranes, and identify engineered H 2 -catalytic membranes as a promising low-energy technology for destructive PFAS treatment.
